primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Reported performance gains (e.g., 99.6% mAP@0.5, 94.2% mAP@0.5:0.95, and substantial box loss reduction) are backed by aligned tabular and graphical evidence across comparable baselines, with consistent improvements shown across one-stage and two-stage detector families.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The evaluation is rigorous and multifaceted: the proposed loss is benchmarked against eight existing IoU-based loss variants (IoU, GIoU, DIoU, CIoU, SIoU, EIoU, WIoU, Shape-IoU) on the OAI dataset, evaluated across 9 different one-stage and two-stage detectors, verified via ablation of distance normalization, statistically analyzed across multiple random seeds with 95% confidence intervals, evaluated on an external dataset, and checked for patient-level split leakage.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Evaluations on a held-out test split, an external digital knee X-ray dataset, and a strict patient-level partitioned test set demonstrate consistent high performance (mAP@0.5:0.95 of 92.8% on the external dataset and 92.8% under patient-level partitioning).
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Standard COCO-style object detection evaluation metrics (Precision, Recall, mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95) computed on held-out test datasets.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Supervised gradient descent backpropagation using task loss combining LD-IoU regression loss and classification losses on training image partitions.

primary.limitations: The authors explicitly address key limitations, noting that initial experiments relied on Kaggle OAI image-level splits, confirming robustness via patient-level splits and external dataset testing, while noting that future work remains needed for larger multi-center cohorts and modalities such as MRI/CT.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is thoroughly formulated mathematically: the authors define center-point Lorentzian distance, its scale-invariant normalization based on the smallest enclosing bounding box, and its integration into the regression loss. Implementation details, including hyperparameter settings, dataset split protocols, and optimization procedures across Ultralytics YOLOv8 and MMDetection frameworks, are clearly specified.
primary.quality_rationale: The manuscript presents a clearly motivated, mathematically sound, and thoroughly benchmarked localization loss. The extensive comparative evaluation against current state-of-the-art IoU variants and diverse model architectures, along with ablation, multi-seed statistical testing, and data leakage checks, demonstrates scientific rigor justifying admission.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper introduces LD-IoU (Lorentzian Distance Intersection over Union), a scale-invariant bounding-box regression loss function that integrates normalized Lorentzian distance into the standard IoU formulation to improve localization and convergence in YOLOv8 and other object detection frameworks for knee osteoarthritis severity detection.

The anchor grid sets the maximum candidate
count, so a cap validated on one output tensor
says little about another. We repeated the capture
and the sweep on the same detector family with-
out its P2 head: 33,600 anchors against 136,000,
a factor of four in the quantity that sets the
ceiling. K = 1024 holds the suppression budget
on both, 3.11 ms against 4.19 ms in the same
run, while the runtime's shipped ceiling of 30,000
misses on both, at 187.30 and 342.96 ms. This is
suppression replay only; no accuracy claim is made
for the second model, and the bound is estab-
lished for the two geometries tested rather than
for anchor-based detectors in general.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: The headline suppression-latency reduction is corroborated by objective wall-clock measurements across three independent backends, a second detector geometry, a second corpus, and an edge board, while the accuracy cost is measured on held-out test-dev data.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Client-observed and stage-isolated p95 wall-clock latency, deadline-miss ratio, and held-out COCO-style AP@[.50:.95] on the exported artifact.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Projected gradient ascent on a differentiable surrogate for pre-NMS candidate count, plus a grid-swept calibration rule selecting K from measured tail latency and an accuracy tolerance.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims match the reported measurements with exemplary precision: the paper shows bounded admission successfully confines NMS tail latency (e.g., to 4.28 ms at K=1024), while candidly demonstrating that end-to-end deadline integrity fails due to input decoding overhead rather than candidate handling.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The empirical evaluation is rigorous and multi-faceted, testing multiple anchor configurations, two vision corpora (VisDrone and BDD100K), thermal throttling on an edge platform (Raspberry Pi 4B), and end-to-end client-observed tail latencies with matched lossless image controls.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Evaluations rely on objective physical clock measurements across three distinct backends, edge hardware, and held-out test datasets.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Client-observed and stage-isolated p95 wall-clock latency, deadline-miss ratio (DMR), and held-out COCO-style AP@[0.50:0.95] across multiple independent suppression runtimes and hardware platforms.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Projected gradient ascent on anchor confidence scores for generating adversarial candidate inflation, and an analytical calibration rule over swept candidate grids to determine the admission bound K*.

primary.limitations: The authors explicitly report threats to validity, noting that K* calibration was conducted over limited sessions, that millisecond timings are target-specific rather than formal WCET bounds, and that bounding suppression work is insufficient by itself to secure the end-to-end serving pipeline.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is thoroughly detailed, implementing a deterministic projected gradient ascent attack targeting pre-NMS anchor expansion, replaying captured arrays across three distinct suppression backends (NumPy CPU, torchvision CPU, and torchvision CUDA), and instrumenting both stage-local and end-to-end client latencies.
primary.quality_rationale: This work provides a sound, highly transparent, and realistic systems-level evaluation of latency attacks and defenses in real-time object detection, characterized by honest negative findings regarding end-to-end client deadlines and fully documented artifacts.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper demonstrates that candidate-inflation latency attacks against object detection remain attacker-controlled across backends, and establishes a deployment-calibrated candidate admission bound (K) prior to NMS that strictly limits suppression latency while quantifying its minimal clean accuracy cost.

blocking_reasons: The manuscript contains no completed empirical validation: FPGA implementation metrics and detection accuracy (mAP) results are presented as 'TBD' placeholders.

The reported synthesis attempt produced zero retained cells because the testbench was used as the synthesis top, yielding 0.0 W dynamic power and an empty device view, so no functioning accelerator was demonstrated.

The behavioral simulation does not demonstrate an executed accelerator transaction because start and done remain low, and the claimed hardware correctness cannot be verified from the captured waveform.
Headline performance and storage figures are explicitly labeled as pre-synthesis analytical estimates rather than measured results, leaving the central efficiency claims unsupported.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: No evaluator-independent measurement is possible because the manuscript contains only analytical estimates and incomplete synthesis or simulation outputs with no dataset-level accuracy or post-route resource results.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Analytical throughput and storage formulas, along with preliminary and largely inactive Vivado synthesis and simulation reports.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Analytical design choices such as channel-group precision assignment and lane-fusion scheduling.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: The paper transparently acknowledges that the presented numerical results are pre-synthesis analytical estimates and template placeholders, but this leaves the substantive empirical claims completely unvalidated.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The empirical evaluation is largely absent or filled with placeholder template values ('TBD'). Synthesis yielded zero retained cells and 0.0 W dynamic power, behavioral simulation captured an inactive state without execution, and no object detection accuracy (mAP) or hardware benchmark figures were measured.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: All experimental tables (Table A1 and Table A2) contain 'TBD' placeholders, and no completed synthesis, board measurements, or mAP evaluation were executed.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Vivado synthesis/simulation reports and proposed object detection evaluation templates (PASCAL VOC / COCO mAP and timing metrics).
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Analytical throughput formulas and sensitivity-based channel-group precision assignment.

primary.limitations: The authors explicitly disclose that actual synthesis, power measurements, board-level execution, and detector accuracy tests on datasets like COCO or VOC were not completed.
primary.method_assessment: The architecture introduces conceptual designs for 16-channel grouped precision and a 64-PE array with 4-slice fusible processing elements. However, the hardware description and implementation are incomplete, as synthesis failed to retain logic due to setting the testbench as the synthesis top.
primary.quality_rationale: Scientific promotion requires meaningful evaluation or empirical validation. Because the RTL implementation was not properly synthesized, verified, or benchmarked, and the experimental tables contain only placeholders, scientific confidence cannot be established.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper proposes FlexXNOR-OD, an FPGA accelerator architecture combining channel-grouped precision assignment (1, 2, 4, or 8 bits) with lane-fusible XNOR processing elements for edge object detection.

scholarly_quality.rationale: Scientific promotion requires meaningful evaluation or empirical validation. Because the RTL implementation was not properly synthesized, verified, or benchmarked, and the experimental tables contain only placeholders, scientific confidence cannot be established.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors explicitly disclose that actual synthesis, power measurements, board-level execution, and detector accuracy tests on datasets like COCO or VOC were not completed.

blocking_reasons: The claimed controlled comparison is undermined by differing training configurations across models, including different loss functions and epoch budgets, so the comparison is not actually under identical conditions.

Headline results are selected from peak validation checkpoints, and no independent held-out test split evaluation is reported, leaving the reported gains measured in the same signal used for checkpoint selection.
Reported final metrics are internally inconsistent, with TransUNet stated as 0.67 mIoU / 0.52 Dice in results but 0.64 mIoU / 0.54 Dice in the conclusion.

evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Gradient-descent loss optimization and peak validation mIoU used for checkpoint selection.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims regarding model performance and generalization are only supported by validation set curves from a mixed dataset. Numerical inconsistencies exist, such as reporting TransUNet peak metrics as 0.67 mIoU / 0.52 Dice in text and tables versus 0.64 mIoU / 0.54 Dice in the conclusion.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The evaluation relies on tracking validation mIoU and Dice scores to select best checkpoints. While a 10% test split was partitioned, no standalone held-out test split evaluation metrics or uncertainty estimates (such as standard deviations across runs or per-dataset breakdowns) are reported, as headline metrics merely reflect peak validation epoch checkpoints.

primary.limitations: The authors acknowledge limitations including hardware intensity, dataset scale dependency, restriction to binary segmentation, and absence of real-world inference speed or deployment testing.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology pools three distinct benchmark datasets into a single 8,304-image collection and applies standard preprocessing, augmentation, and architectures. However, hyperparameter choices such as loss functions, batch sizes, and epoch budgets differ arbitrarily across architectures (e.g., Cross-Entropy for ViT vs Dice Loss for U-Net and TransUNet), undermining the claim of a controlled, unified experimental setup.
primary.quality_rationale: The study evaluates standard public architectures on pooled benchmark data without proposing architectural or methodological innovations. Inconsistent training configurations between compared models, conflation of validation checkpoint picking with final testing, lack of cross-run variance, and contradictory reporting of final metrics warrant an uncertain assessment.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper provides an empirical comparison of three deep learning architectures (U-Net, ViT, and TransUNet) trained and evaluated under unified conditions across three merged industrial surface defect benchmarks (MVTec AD, NEU, and DAGM 2007).
